title: Crash Avoidance & Hazards
summary: How to stop hard, swerve, take curves, cross bad surfaces and handle breakdowns, animals and flying objects without crashing.

blocks.text: Stopping fast and swerving are the two key crash-avoidance skills. Crash studies show most crash-involved riders underbrake the front tire, overbrake the rear, and either do not separate braking from swerving or do not choose to swerve when they should.

items: Use both brakes at the same time. The front brake can provide 70% or more of your stopping power.
Squeeze the front lever firmly and progressively. Do not be shy with it, but never grab it.
Keep your body centered over the motorcycle and look well ahead, not down.
For maximum straight-line braking, apply both brakes fully without locking either wheel.

rows: Front wheel locks
Release the front brake at once, then reapply it smoothly with less pressure. A front skid means instant loss of steering and balance; not releasing it leads to a crash.
Rear wheel locks, bike upright and straight
On a good traction surface you can keep it locked until you have completely stopped. You can still control the bike.
Rear wheel locks and slides out of line
Releasing it can cause a high-side crash: the bike snaps upright and throws you off. Even slight misalignment can do this.

blocks.text: Too much rear brake locks the rear wheel, and once it locks you can no longer change direction.
When the motorcycle is leaned over, part of your traction is used for cornering. Less is left for braking, so too much brake can cause a skid. Squeeze the levers; never grab.

items: Best choice: straighten the motorcycle and square the handlebars first, then stop.
If straightening would carry you into danger (oncoming traffic in a right-hand curve, or off the road in a left-hand curve), brake smoothly and gradually while still leaned.
As you slow, reduce your lean and add more brake until the bike is straight and you can use full braking.
Always straighten the handlebars in the last few feet of the stop so you stay balanced and upright.

blocks.text: Sometimes there is not enough room to stop, even with both brakes used correctly. Then a swerve, a quick change of direction, may be the only way to avoid a crash.

items: Press the handgrip on the side you want to escape toward. Press right to go right, left to go left. The bike leans quickly that way.
Keep your body upright and let the motorcycle lean underneath you. Knees against the tank, feet firmly on the footrests.
Look at your escape path, not at the obstacle.
Once you are clear, press the opposite handgrip to return to your original direction.

blocks.text: Do not brake during an aggressive swerve. If the situation allows, brake before the swerve or after it.
Running wide in a curve or turn is a primary cause of single-vehicle motorcycle crashes. Ride within your skill level and the posted speed.

items: Every curve is different. It may stay constant, widen, get tighter, or turn into several curves.

A good choice is to move to the center of your lane before the curve and stay there until you exit. You see oncoming traffic sooner and can adjust for cars crowding the center line or debris in your lane.
Your best path may not follow the curve of the road. Change lane position for traffic, road conditions and the shape of the curve.

blocks.text: Avoid bumps, potholes and road trash by slowing or going around them. If you must ride over a small obstacle:

items: Slow down as much as you can before contact.
Approach as close to a 90-degree angle as possible, with the motorcycle straight.
Rise slightly off the seat with your weight on the footrests so your knees and elbows absorb the shock.
Just before the front tire hits, roll on the throttle slightly to lighten the front end, then roll off.
Afterward, pull off the road and check your tires and rims for damage before riding farther.

rows: Tracks crossing at an angle
Usually ride straight across within your lane. Turning to meet them at 90 degrees can put you into another lane.
Tracks, ruts or seams running parallel to you
Move far enough away to cross at an angle of at least 45 degrees, then make a deliberate turn so you are not thrown off balance.
Rain grooves and bridge gratings
The bike may weave. This wandering feeling is generally not hazardous. Relax, keep a steady speed and ride straight across. Zigzagging is far more dangerous.

items: Wet pavement, especially just after rain starts, before surface oil washes to the side of the road.
Gravel roads and places where sand and gravel collect, including road edges on curves and ramps.
Mud, leaves, snow and ice.
Painted lane markings, steel plates and surface covers, especially when wet.

blocks.caption: Painted lane lines give poor traction, especially when wet.

items: Slow down before you reach the slippery spot, especially before wet curves. You need more distance to stop.
Avoid sudden changes in speed or direction. Be smooth when you accelerate, shift, turn or brake.
Use both brakes with gentle pressure. The front brake still works; squeeze it gradually so the front wheel does not lock.
When rain starts, ride in the tire tracks left by vehicles, often the left track. The center of the lane can be slick.
Watch for oil spots when you put your foot down at a stop.

blocks.text: Patches of ice tend to develop in low or shaded areas and on bridges and overpasses, and wet leaves are just as slippery. If you cannot avoid ice or snow, keep the bike straight up and go as slowly as possible. At a walking pace, let your feet skim the surface, stay off the brakes, and if possible squeeze the clutch and coast.

rows: Flat front tire
Steering feels heavy. Especially dangerous because you need steering to keep your balance.
Flat rear tire
The back of the bike jerks or sways side to side.
Either tire flat

Hold the grips firmly, ease off the throttle and keep a straight course. If you must brake, gradually use the brake on the good tire, if you are sure which one it is. Then edge to the roadside, squeeze the clutch and stop.
Stuck throttle

If the situation allows, twist it back and forth several times to free it. If it stays stuck, immediately hit the engine cut-off switch and squeeze the clutch together. Power to the rear wheel stops even if the engine sound does not drop right away. Move to a safe area and stop, and make sure the throttle works freely before riding again.
Chain or belt breaks
You lose power to the rear wheel instantly. Close the throttle and brake to a stop in a safe area. A chain or belt that slips or breaks can also lock the rear wheel and cause a skid.
Drive shaft
Loss of oil in the rear differential can lock the rear wheel, and you may not be able to prevent a skid.
Engine seizure

Usually caused by low oil. The first sign may be lost power or a changed engine sound. Squeeze the clutch to disconnect the engine from the rear wheel, pull off and stop. Check the oil and let the engine cool before restarting. A seized engine acts like a locked rear wheel.

blocks.text: A wobble is when the front wheel and handlebars suddenly shake from side to side, at any speed. Trying to accelerate out of it only makes the motorcycle more unstable. If a wobble starts:

items: Grip the handlebars firmly, but do not fight the wobble.
Close the throttle gradually. Do not brake, which can make it worse, and do not try to accelerate out of it.
Move your weight as far forward and down as possible.
Pull off the road as soon as you can and fix the problem.

rows: Most common causes
Improper loading, unsuitable accessories or incorrect tire pressure.
Fix the load and settings

Lighten or reposition a heavy load, centering it lower and farther forward. Set tire pressure, spring preload, air shocks and dampers for the weight you carry. Make sure windshields and fairings are mounted properly.
Then check the hardware
Poorly adjusted or worn steering parts, a bent, misaligned or out-of-balance front wheel, loose wheel bearings or spokes, and worn swingarm bearings.
Still not found
Have the motorcycle checked thoroughly by a qualified professional.

sections.heading: Animals, flying objects and leaving the road

rows: Small animal in traffic
Do what you safely can to avoid it, but stay in your lane. Hitting something small is less dangerous than hitting a car.
Dog chasing you
Downshift and approach it slowly, then speed up and leave it behind. Never kick at it.
Deer, elk or cattle
Brake and prepare to stop. Large animals are unpredictable.
Insect, pebble or cigarette hits you
Keep your eyes on the road and your hands on the handlebars. Pull off to fix any damage when it is safe.

items: Check the roadside. If it is soft grass, loose sand or you are not sure, slow way down before turning onto it.
Signal clearly, check your mirror and do a head check before slowing or turning off.
Get as far off the road as you can. A motorcycle at the roadside is hard to see, and another driver may pull off in the same spot.
Park carefully. Loose or sloped shoulders make it hard to use the side or center stand.

keyPoints: Stop quickly with both brakes; squeeze the front firmly but never grab it.
Front wheel locks: release the brake immediately, then reapply smoothly with less pressure. Rear locks while upright and straight: you may keep it locked to a stop.
To swerve, press the grip on the side you want to go, look at your escape path, and never brake during the swerve.
In a curve, straighten before a hard stop when you can, and always square the bars in the last few feet.
Cross obstacles near 90 degrees, angled tracks straight in your lane, and parallel seams at 45 degrees or more.
On slick roads slow down, stay smooth, use both brakes gently, and ride in the tire tracks when rain starts.
In a wobble, grip firmly, close the throttle gradually, shift your weight forward and down, and do not brake or accelerate.
Stay in your lane for small animals in traffic, but brake and prepare to stop for large ones like deer.
